data.stem: For how long does the Comptroller and Auditor General of India hold office?
options: Six years or until age 65, whichever is earlier
Until age 65, with no fixed term
Six years or until age 70, whichever is later
data.explanation: Six years or until age 65, whichever is earlier, is correct under the Constitution's provision for the CAG. A five-year term, a term with no fixed limit and a retirement age of 70 are all wrong, since the CAG's tenure ends at the earlier of six years or age 65.
data.label: practice

data.stem: Which post holder heads the Indian Audit and Accounts Department?
options: The Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee
The Comptroller and Auditor General of India
data.explanation: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is correct, because the CAG heads the Indian Audit and Accounts Department under Article 148. The Cabinet Secretary leads the government's secretariat, the PAC chairman holds a parliamentary post, and the Finance Secretary runs a ministry department, so those options are incorrect.
data.label: practice

data.stem: Who appoints the Comptroller and Auditor General of India?
options: The President, by warrant under hand and seal
data.explanation: The President is correct: the CAG is appointed by a warrant under hand and seal, and the CAG then takes an oath before the President. The Prime Minister, a joint resolution of Parliament and the Chief Justice have no role in the appointment, so those options are wrong.
data.label: practice

data.stem: Under which Article is the independent office of the Comptroller and Auditor General created?
data.explanation: Article 148 is correct: it creates the independent office of the CAG. Article 76 creates the Attorney General of India, Article 151 governs the audit reports, and Article 165 creates the Advocate General of a state, so those options are wrong.
data.label: practice

data.stem: Which arrangement keeps the CAG's office expenses outside the annual vote of Parliament?
options: Administrative expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
Its budget is voted every year by the Lok Sabha
The Finance Ministry fixes its salary each year
The Public Accounts Committee approves its staff
data.explanation: Charging the administrative expenses on the Consolidated Fund of India is correct, since those expenses are then not subject to the vote of Parliament. An annual Lok Sabha vote, an annual salary decision by the Finance Ministry and PAC approval of staff all cut against the office's independence, so they are wrong.
data.label: practice

data.stem:
Consider the following statements about the Comptroller and Auditor General of India:
1. Removal needs a special-majority resolution of both Houses of Parliament, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
2. After leaving office, the CAG may hold any post under the Government of India.
3. The salary of the CAG is the same as that of a Supreme Court judge.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
data.explanation: 1 and 3 only is correct: removal needs a special-majority resolution of both Houses on proved misbehaviour or incapacity, and the salary matches a Supreme Court judge's. Statement 2 is wrong because the CAG is barred from any further office under the Union or a state, so every option that includes statement 2 is incorrect.
data.label: practice

data.stem: Which of these tasks is NOT a constitutional role of the Comptroller and Auditor General?
options: Advising the President on the form in which the Union and state accounts are kept
Certifying the net proceeds of a tax or duty
Acting as guide, friend and philosopher to the Public Accounts Committee
Deciding the rate of income tax to be levied each year
data.explanation: Deciding the rate of income tax each year is correct as the NOT answer, because tax rates are set by Parliament through the budget and the Finance Act, not by the CAG. The other three are real CAG roles under Articles 150 and 279 and in relation to the PAC, so they are wrong.
data.label: practice

data.stem: Under Article 151, to whom does the CAG send audit reports on state accounts?
options: The Chief Minister of the state
The Speaker of the state assembly
data.explanation: The Governor is correct: the Governor places the state audit reports before the state legislature. The Chief Minister and the Speaker are not in the reporting chain, and reports on state accounts never go to the President, who receives only the Union reports, so those options are wrong.
data.label: practice

data.stem: In which year was the CAG relieved of compiling the accounts of the Central Government?
data.explanation: 1976 is correct: the accounts were separated from audit that year through departmentalisation, and the CAG stopped compiling central accounts. The year 1971 saw the CAG's duties Act passed, 1986 has no link to this change, and 2006 is when performance audit was confirmed, so those years are wrong.
data.label: practice

data.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the three audit reports the CAG submits to the President?
options: Audit report on the Union Public Service Commission
data.explanation: The report on the Union Public Service Commission is correct as the NOT answer, because it is not a CAG report at all; the UPSC is a separate constitutional body. The appropriation, finance and public undertakings reports are the three the CAG submits to the President, so those options are wrong.
data.label: practice

data.stem:
Consider the following statements about the propriety audit conducted by the CAG:
1. It is compulsory for the CAG to conduct it every year.
2. It examines the wisdom, faithfulness and economy of government expenditure.
3. It can comment on wasteful and extravagant spending.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
data.explanation: 2 and 3 only is correct: propriety audit looks at wisdom, faithfulness and economy, and it can comment on waste and extravagance. Statement 1 is wrong because propriety audit is discretionary, while the legal and regulatory audit is the compulsory one, so options containing statement 1 are incorrect.
data.label: practice

data.stem:
Consider the following statements about the audit powers of the CAG:
1. It may inspect any office or department that is subject to its audit.
2. It decides the extent and manner of an audit.
3. It can stop a department from drawing money by cheque until an audit is complete.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
data.explanation: 1 and 2 only is correct: the CAG may inspect audited offices and decide how far and how the audit proceeds. Statement 3 is wrong because the CAG does not gatekeep spending: departments draw money without its prior authority, and its role begins only at audit, so options with statement 3 are incorrect.
data.label: practice

data.stem: How does the CAG of India differ from the CAG of Britain in controlling the drawing of public money?
options: The Indian CAG approves each withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund before it is made
The Indian CAG does not approve withdrawals, whereas the British CAG must approve them
The British CAG audits receipts only, while the Indian CAG audits expenditure
Both auditors approve every withdrawal from the public exchequer
data.explanation: The Indian CAG does not approve withdrawals, whereas the British CAG must approve them, is correct: in India departments draw money without prior CAG sanction, while in Britain the executive can draw only with CAG approval. The first and fourth options wrongly give the Indian CAG or both a prior approval role, and the third misstates the audit scope, so they are wrong.
data.label: practice

data.stem: Which category of public corporation is audited only by private auditors, with the CAG having no role at all?
options: Corporations audited totally and directly by the CAG
Corporations audited by private auditors appointed in consultation with the CAG
Corporations subject to totally private audit, which report directly to Parliament
Government companies audited by the CAG alone under the Companies Act
data.explanation: Corporations subject to totally private audit is correct: their accounts are audited exclusively by private auditors, and the CAG is absent from that process. Direct CAG audit and the consultation model both involve the CAG, and government companies are not audited by the CAG alone, so those options are wrong.
data.label: practice

data.stem: According to the Second Administrative Reforms Commission, roughly how many audit paras in a year's CAG reports receive detailed examination by the Public Accounts Committee?
data.explanation: Around 15 to 20 is correct: against 1000 to 1500 paras in the CAG's annual reports, the PAC examines only about that many in detail. The other figures overstate the examination, and the claim that every para is examined contradicts the Commission's finding, so those options are wrong.
data.label: practice

data.stem: Which instrument placed performance audit within the scope of the CAG's work in 2006?
options: A judgment of the Supreme Court
A specification of functions by the President
data.explanation: A Finance Ministry Office Memorandum is correct: it clarified in 2006 that performance audit falls within the CAG's scope. The 1971 Act came decades earlier and did not introduce this change, while a court judgment and a presidential specification were not the instruments used, so those options are wrong.
data.label: practice

data.stem: What does the CAG's certificate on the net proceeds of a tax or duty under Article 279 signify?
options: It is advisory and the Finance Minister may overrule it on review
It is final; net proceeds are proceeds minus the cost of collection
It is provisional and lapses when the next budget is presented
It covers gross receipts, including the cost of collecting them
data.explanation: The second option is correct: the CAG's certificate under Article 279 is final, and net proceeds means the proceeds minus the cost of collection. The advisory, provisional and gross-receipt options each get either the finality or the definition wrong, so they are incorrect.
data.label: practice

data.stem:
Consider the following statements about the audit reports under Article 151:
1. Reports on Union accounts go to the President, who lays them before Parliament.
2. Reports on state accounts go to the Governor, who places them before the state legislature.
3. The Speaker of the Lok Sabha presents Union reports to Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
data.explanation: 1 and 2 only is correct, because the President lays Union reports before Parliament and the Governor places state reports before the state legislature. Statement 3 is wrong since the Speaker has no part in this chain, so options that include statement 3 are incorrect.
data.label: practice

data.stem: The salary of the CAG is equal to that of which constitutional office holder, and who determines it?
options: A High Court chief justice; fixed by the President by rules
A Union minister; fixed by the Finance Commission
A Cabinet Secretary; fixed by the President
A Supreme Court judge; fixed by Parliament through an Act
data.explanation: A Supreme Court judge, with the salary fixed by Parliament through an Act, is correct. The other options name a different office or a different fixing authority, so they are wrong.
data.label: practice

data.stem: Which condition of the CAG's service is protected from change to the CAG's disadvantage after appointment?
options: Membership of the Public Accounts Committee
A seat in the Rajya Sabha
data.explanation: Pension is correct: salary, leave, pension and age of retirement cannot be altered to the CAG's disadvantage after appointment. Membership of the Public Accounts Committee, a ministerial portfolio and a Rajya Sabha seat are not protected terms of the office, so those options are wrong.
data.label: practice

data.stem: Which Article empowers the CAG to advise the President on the form of the government accounts?
data.explanation: Article 150 is correct: it covers the form in which the accounts of the Union and the states are kept, on the CAG's advice to the President. Article 149 deals with the CAG's duties and powers, Article 151 with audit reports, and Article 279 with the net proceeds certificate, so those options are wrong.
data.label: practice

data.stem:
Consider the following statements about the functions of the CAG:
1. It audits the accounts of government companies in accordance with the Companies Act.
2. It still compiles and maintains the accounts of the Central Government as a routine task.
3. It audits the accounts of bodies that receive grants and loans for specific purposes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
data.explanation: 1 and 3 only is correct: government companies are audited under the Companies Act, and bodies receiving grants and loans for specific purposes fall within the audit. Statement 2 is wrong because the CAG was relieved of compiling central accounts in 1976, although it still compiles state accounts, so options containing statement 2 are incorrect.
data.label: practice
